analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal discount program for prescription drugs for people without drug coverage, funded by manufacturer rebates.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 39 cosponsors but was referred to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set up an 'America Rx' program run by the Department of Health and Human Services giving discounted prescription drug prices to US residents who have no other drug coverage. Drug manufacturers would have had to pay rebates to the government, similar in size to the rebates companies already pay under Medicaid, and those rebates would reimburse pharmacies for the discounts they give. To push manufacturers to sign rebate agreements, the bill would deny them the federal tax deduction for their drug advertising and marketing expenses if they refused. The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in April 2003 and then to its Health subcommittee, where it sat for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: US citizens, permanent residents, seniors, and people with disabilities who lack any public or private program covering prescription drugs. They would get discounted prices at participating pharmacies, with rebates from drug makers covering most of the cost. The bill also requires screening applicants for Medicaid eligibility so they can be enrolled in programs they qualify for.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured residents paying full drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Directs HHS to establish a program providing qualified US residents access to discounted outpatient prescription drug prices.

Requires the Secretary to negotiate manufacturer rebate agreements averaging rebates comparable to those obtained under the Medicaid drug rebate program, with rebates paid to pharmacies that provide the discounts.

Guarantees participating pharmacies prompt reimbursement of discounts plus a reasonable dispensing fee, and forbids extra fees on pharmacies, so discounts reach patients without pharmacies absorbing the cost.
Requires outreach, simplified eligibility procedures, and uniform eligibility standards to maximize enrollment of qualified residents.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would pay rebates comparable to Medicaid's and lose the tax deduction for drug advertising and marketing expenses if they refused to sign rebate agreements. The public Treasury funds administration, though rebates are designated to cover program costs.

drawbacks.text: The program only covers people with no other drug coverage, so it does not lower prices for anyone with insurance or Medicare drug benefits, and it does nothing to change list prices for the broader market.

The rebate level is pegged to Medicaid's average, and the compliance mechanism is a tax penalty on advertising expenses rather than direct price authority, which manufacturers and their allies would have argued is a blunt and legally contested way to force participation.

Because the discount reflects rebates minus administrative costs, and federal and state governments fund administration and outreach, actual patient discounts depend on program execution, and the bill's design leaves the discount method largely to the Secretary to specify.

Coverage-based drug benefits could be crowded out: the bill acknowledges in its findings that it does not want to discourage employer or insurer coverage, but a free discount program for the uninsured creates some risk that employers drop drug coverage to shift employees onto it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem—people with no drug coverage paying full retail prices—with a mechanism already proven in Medicaid: manufacturer rebates passed through to point-of-sale discounts. The costs fall mainly on manufacturers rather than taxpayers, and pharmacies are protected with guaranteed reimbursement. The design is narrower and less powerful than direct price negotiation; it helps one slice of the population rather than lowering drug prices generally, and enforcement rests on a tax penalty whose durability was uncertain. Still, on its own terms it offered clear benefits to a vulnerable group at concentrated industry cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee in April 2003, and it stayed there until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005 without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 9, 2003, by Rep. Michael Michaud with 30 original cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On April 24, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, its last recorded action in the Congress.
The bill accumulated 39 cosponsors (38 Democrats and 1 Independent) but never advanced past the subcommittee and received no vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: they never had to pay the negotiated rebates or give up their advertising tax deduction, and people without drug coverage got no relief. Congress instead addressed drug benefits that same period through different legislation that did not use this rebate mechanism.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers; uninsured got nothing

for.name: Rep. Michael H. Michaud
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 39 cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it was sent to the Health subcommittee and never came out.

against.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair during the 108th Congress, oversaw the panel that took no action on the bill; weeks after leaving Congress in 2004 he became president of PhRMA, the drug industry's lobby.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernard Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would have required rebates averaging Medicaid levels and denied the advertising tax deduction to manufacturers that refused rebate agreements. The bill's death meant no rebate obligation and no loss of the tax break.
Pharmacies that joined the program would have received prompt reimbursement for discounts plus a dispensing fee and no additional participation fees, with rebates covering the cost of discounts.
The Secretary and states could contract with pharmacy benefit managers and other third parties to administer eligibility and pharmacy arrangements.
